title: Hairpin lace stole
subtitle: Hairpin lace strips joined with slip stitch to make a 190 cm x 50 cm stole in DK on a 4 mm hook
excerpt: Hairpin lace is worked on a U-shaped frame tool, not a standard crochet hook alone. The frame holds two prongs a set distance apart; you wind yarn around the prongs and work a central crochet spine to produce a strip of looped lace. This stole joins five strips side by side with slip stitch joins to reach 190 cm long by 50 cm wide.
sourceNotes: Hairpin lace construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1889-1890), which describes the use of a staple or fork frame to produce looped braid strips. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), also describes fork crochet (Internet Archive).
heroPrompt: A hairpin lace stole in natural DK wool draped over a wooden chair back, the loop-edged strips and slip-stitch joins clearly visible in soft afternoon light.

crochet.gaugeText: Each hairpin lace strip measures approximately 10 cm wide (50 mm between prongs) x 190 cm long, after joining. 20 loops per 10 cm along the strip length.
crochet.finishedSizeText: Approximately 190 cm long x 50 cm wide (5 strips joined), after blocking.

glossaryTerms.definition: A U-shaped tool with two parallel prongs set a fixed distance apart (typically 5 cm, 7.5 cm, or 10 cm) and a connecting bar. The yarn winds around the prongs while a crochet hook works a chain spine down the centre. The frame can be purchased from specialist crochet suppliers.
A completed length of hairpin lace: a central chain spine flanked on each side by rows of loops. The loops on each edge are later used to join strips together.

The slip-stitch method of linking adjacent hairpin lace strips. Working along the inner edges of two strips simultaneously, you draw up loops from both sides and sl st them together to form a flat seam.

content.text: Hairpin lace requires a
hairpin lace frame

in addition to a standard 4 mm crochet hook. The frame is a separate specialist tool that holds two prongs 50 mm apart; without it, the stitch cannot be worked. Frames are sold by crochet suppliers and haberdashery shops, often as adjustable sets with multiple prong spacings. Set the prong spacing to 50 mm before beginning.
The stole is made from five
hairpin lace strips
, each 190 cm long with 380 loops per side (20 loops per 10 cm). The five strips are joined flat using a
loop join
along each shared inner edge. The outer edges of the two border strips are left as open loops, giving the stole its characteristic fringe-like lace finish.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 350 g DK-weight yarn (a smooth, slightly plied yarn shows the loops clearly; avoid very fuzzy fibres which obscure the lace structure). A 4 mm crochet hook (US G/6). A hairpin lace frame set to 50 mm prong spacing -- sold separately by crochet suppliers. Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.

attrs.title: Hairpin frame note
attrs.body: Hairpin lace frames are not included in a standard crochet kit. They are available from specialist crochet suppliers and haberdashery shops, typically sold as a set of prong pairs with a connecting bar. Adjustable metal frames (e.g. 25 mm to 100 mm prong spacing) cover the full range of lace widths and are the most practical option. Confirm the 50 mm setting on your specific frame before casting on.

content.text: Gauge

20 loops per 10 cm along the length of the strip, with the frame set at 50 mm prong spacing. Work 20 cm of your first strip, count the loops along one edge, and adjust the tension of your central chain spine if the count does not match. A tighter spine produces more loops per 10 cm and a shorter strip; a looser spine produces fewer loops and a longer strip.
Stitches used
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared. Used in the central spine and in the strip joins.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used in the central spine of each strip and in the edging.
Hairpin lace basic
: yarn wound around prong then dc in central spine -- the core move of the frame-based technique.
Pattern
Starting each strip

Make a slip knot and place it on the 4 mm hook. Hold the frame with the two prongs in your non-hook hand. Drape the yarn over the left prong from front to back, then work 1 dc into the loop on the hook, drawing the yarn through. Turn the frame 180 degrees from left to right (the right prong now faces left). The yarn wraps around the prong as you turn. Work 1 dc into the two threads of the central loop. Turn the frame again. Continue: each full turn deposits one loop on the outer edge of each prong and each dc forms one link of the central chain spine.
Working each strip to length

Work until each strip has 380 loops on each side (which gives 190 cm at 20 loops per 10 cm). When the strip fills the frame, slip the loops off carefully onto a spare length of yarn or a long stitch holder, then replace them on the frame and continue. Count loops every 50 turns to track progress. Fasten off each strip when the loop count reaches 380 on each side, leaving a 15 cm tail. Make 5 strips total.
Joining strips with loop join
Lay two strips side by side with their inner edges facing. Using the 4 mm hook and the working yarn (or a separate joining length), work the
loop join

: *insert hook into 1 loop from the left strip and 1 loop from the right strip, draw the right-strip loop through the left-strip loop, then sl st*; repeat from * to * along the full length, working one pair of loops per sl st. Work all 380 loop pairs. Repeat for each join between the 5 strips. You will have 4 joins total. (5 strips joined)
Short-end edging

At each short end of the stole, work a row of dc across the 5 strip ends to neaten: join yarn at one corner, ch 1 (does not count as a stitch), work 1 dc into each central spine end across all 5 strips. Fasten off. Repeat at the other short end.
Finishing

Weave in all ends through the central spines of the strips. Wet-block by soaking the joined stole in cool water for 10 minutes, pressing water out gently in a towel, then pinning the two long edges and both short edges to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Leave the outer loop edges free and pin them lightly at intervals to spread them evenly.
Care

Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Lay flat to dry. The open loops are delicate; do not wring or tumble-dry. Check the loop joins after washing and ease any pulled stitches back into place while still damp.
What to try next

Changing the frame width to 75 mm produces wider strips and a more open lace appearance from the same loop count. Working the central spine in a contrast colour so it reads differently from the loops is a well-established hairpin variation. A shorter version using three strips produces a narrower scarf rather than a full stole.
